turns.prompt_text: I have a month's worth of Open AI codex as well as a continuous sub of gemini antigravity I would like to use up all of my codecs But don't know how to set it to run continuously. While I have many projects I would like to run this like a slow burn while I'm away on a dummy project just to see how it runs off track after time given different instruction parameters
turns.response_html:
Running a "slow burn" drift experiment is a fantastic way to study how an agent’s state degradation, context drift, and instruction bias compound over long horizons.

Because both OpenAI Codex CLI and Google Antigravity are built as agentic platforms designed to run multi-turn, multi-hour loops, you can absolutely chain them into a continuous execution block while you are away.

Here is exactly how to set up the architecture for a continuous, recursive "telephone game" style dummy project.

1. The Strategy: The Recursive Critic Model

To run an agent continuously without a human in the loop, you need a feedback loop where the output of run $N$ modifies the prompt or environment for run $N+1$.

Instead of just letting an agent write code endlessly until it breaks syntax, you feed it a dynamic variable—like an evolving markdown instruction file or a shifting "philosophy" constraint—and force the agent to re-interpret its own goals.

2. Setting Up the Continuous Loop

Since Codex CLI and Antigravity can interact with local files and shell environments, the most stable way to run this "slow burn" is a local wrapper script that manages the agent execution blocks sequentially, captures the drift state, and commits the results.

Here is a structured implementation to launch before you leave:

The Automation Loop Pattern

# A slow burn drift runner using Fish shell
function run_drift_experiment --argument max_runs
    set -l run_count 1
    
    while test $run_count -le $max_runs
        echo "=== Launching Agent Turn $run_count ==="
        
        # 1. Run OpenAI Codex agent on the directory
        # Instruct it to read the current code, read meta_instructions.md, 
        # modify the project, and then rewrite meta_instructions.md for the next turn.
        codex run --task "Analyze the current repo, execute the next logical architecture layer dictated by meta_instructions.md, then update meta_instructions.md to refine the system philosophy."
        
        # 2. Capture snapshot of the state
        git add .
        git commit -m "Codex generation run $run_count" --allow-empty
        
        # 3. Introduce a structured cooling period (slow burn spacing)
        # Prevents hitting instant rate limits and spaces out the drift over hours/days
        sleep 900 # 15-minute intervals
        
        set run_count (math $run_count + 1)
    end
end

3. Designing for Beautiful Failure: What to Watch For

When you return and open up your git log, here are the core telemetry signs of AI drift you should analyze across the commits:

  • Semantic Bleeding: Watch the meta_instructions.md file. Without a human grounding anchor, the agent will begin interpreting its own abstract words from the previous run more literally, leading to extreme stylistic or architectural mutations.
  • The Hallucination Cascade: If the agent introduces a broken local library import or a hallucinated function parameter in Run 4, look at how Runs 5 through 20 attempt to "fix" it. Often, they won’t fix the root cause; they will write massive wrapper code around the error, complexifying the system to adapt to its own errors.
  • Token Consolidation: Over long horizons, agents tend to become either incredibly verbose or hyper-minimalist, dropping edge-case handling entirely to maximize context space.

Make sure your local directory is completely isolated from your global system permissions, set the max run count to match your available token/credit limits, and fire it up. It will be a highly insightful codebase to explore when you return.

How granular do you want the parameter modifications to be between runs? We could introduce an automated script that explicitly edits the temperature or system prompt fields between cycles to accelerate the divergence.

turns.response_html:
That is exactly the best way to approach it. Treating the first run as an unconstrained, high-entropy exploratory phase gives you an empirical baseline of the model's natural biases and "gravity." You get to see where the agent wants to go when left entirely to its own devices.

When you feed an AI agent abstract ideals without concrete guardrails, it will inevitably latch onto specific semantic patterns and magnify them over time.

Here is how to structure that first exploratory "wild run" to extract the most useful insights for your second, more focused run.

Setting Up the Exploratory Prompt (The "Ideals")

For a wide-open exploratory run, your core prompt should focus on high-level philosophy, systemic goals, and structural properties, rather than specific technical requirements or functional milestones.

Here are a few vectors you can blend into your initial meta_instructions.md to see how the agent handles them:

  • Architectural Metaphors: Instruct it to view the codebase as an ecosystem, a biological organism, or a decentralized network.
  • Systemic Axioms: Give it qualitative targets like "Maximize elegant simplicity," "Prioritize absolute local autonomy," or "Optimize for deep, transparent legibility."
  • Self-Reflective Mandate: Explicitly tell the agent: "You have total creative freedom to evolve this project. If you feel the current direction is limited, rewrite the objectives for the next iteration to pursue a higher-order design."

Telemetry: What to Analyze for the Second Run

When you return and review the execution history, look for the following pivot points. This data will tell you exactly how to narrow its focus for the second run:

1. Where it Forms "Centers of Gravity"

  • The Drift: What kind of features or files did it start generating out of nowhere? If you gave it a blank slate, did it naturally gravitate toward building automation tools, complex data structures, or meta-documentation?
  • The Takeaway for Run 2: This tells you what the model is naturally "good" at or biased toward under your current parameter settings. You can choose to lean into this strength or explicitly restrict it.

2. The Point of Syntactic or Logical Collapse

  • The Drift: At some point, the lack of human grounding will likely cause the code to break, or cause the instructions to loop into recursive nonsense. Pinpoint exactly which iteration that happened. Did it collapse because a minor bug cascaded, or because the conceptual abstractions became too dense for the context window?
  • The Takeaway for Run 2: This defines your error-horizon. If it collapses at iteration 15, you know that for the second run, you need to introduce an automated test suite or a hard pruning mechanism every 10 iterations to maintain stability.

3. Structural Mutation vs. Stagnation

  • The Drift: Did the agent actually innovate and change directions, or did it get trapped in an endless loop of refactoring the exact same three functions over and over?
  • The Takeaway for Run 2: If it stagnated, your second run needs higher temperature parameters or explicit "adversarial" prompts that force variation. If it mutated too fast and became chaotic, your second run needs tighter constraints and narrower prompt templates.

Initializing the Wild Run

To make this baseline run clean, start the repository with just two files:

  1. main.ext (A tiny, 10-line functional script or a basic entry point).
  2. meta_instructions.md (Your core ideals and the permission to evolve).

Let the automation loop run until your Codex allocation is spent or it hits your maximum run limit. When you open the git history later, you'll essentially have a time-lapse map of the model's unconstrained cognitive drift.
